question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
When we speak of biodiversity, most of us picture rainforests teeming with exotic birds and rare orchids. Yet the variety of life matters far less as a spectacle than as a support system. Insects pollinate the crops that feed us, wetlands filter pollutants from water, and microorganisms in the soil recycle dead matter into nutrients. Economists call these benefits ecosystem services, and although nobody sends us a bill for them, replacing them would cost more than any government could afford. The danger is that each species lost weakens the web in ways that are difficult to predict until it is too late. A single predator removed from a forest may allow its prey to multiply unchecked, stripping the vegetation and exposing the soil to erosion. Conservationists therefore argue that protecting nature is not an act of sentiment but of prudence. Critics, however, point out that poor communities living near protected areas often bear the cost of conservation while others enjoy its benefits. A durable solution must, therefore, give these communities a stake in the forest's survival, through employment, shared revenue, and a voice in decisions that affect their lives.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Rare birds and orchids are the most important part of biodiversity
Conservation is an act of sentiment that governments should not fund
Biodiversity is valuable mainly for the vital services it provides, and its protection must involve local communities
Poor communities should be moved away from protected areas

explanation: पैसेज बताता है कि जैव विविधता का असली महत्व उन 'ecosystem services' में है जो वह देती है, और अंत में कहता है कि संरक्षण में स्थानीय समुदायों को भागीदार बनाना होगा। यही दोनों बातें सही विकल्प में हैं।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
For centuries, the artisans of India's villages have produced textiles, pottery and metalware that carried the signature of a region as clearly as its dialect did. The arrival of cheap factory-made goods, however, has pushed many of these crafts to the margins. A handwoven shawl that takes weeks to complete cannot compete on price with a machine-made imitation that appears in the market within hours. Some observers regard this decline as the inevitable price of progress, arguing that societies must let obsolete trades die so that labour can move to more productive work. Others retort that such a view confuses efficiency with value. A craft, they say, is not merely a method of production but a repository of knowledge, passed from one generation to the next, which cannot be recovered once the last practitioner has gone. Several initiatives have therefore sought to rescue these skills by linking artisans directly to urban and overseas buyers, eliminating the middlemen who once pocketed most of the profit. Whether such efforts will succeed depends largely on consumers, who must be willing to pay more for authenticity.

Question: The author's attitude towards the decline of traditional crafts is best described as:

options.text: Indifferent and detached
Concerned, while acknowledging the opposing view
Hostile towards industrialisation
Entirely optimistic about the future

explanation: लेखक शिल्पों के पतन पर चिंता जताते हैं, पर विरोधी मत (अप्रचलित व्यवसायों को मरने देना) को भी निष्पक्ष रूप से रखते हैं; इसलिए 'concerned, yet balanced' सही है।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
The discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century was among the greatest triumphs of medicine, turning once-fatal infections into routine ailments. Yet the same success now threatens to undo itself. Bacteria multiply rapidly, and every time an antibiotic is used, a few organisms may survive by chance mutation and pass their resistance to their offspring. The more frequently a drug is taken, therefore, the faster resistant strains emerge. Misuse accelerates the process: patients who stop a course of treatment as soon as they feel better, doctors who prescribe antibiotics for viral illnesses on which they have no effect, and farmers who feed them routinely to healthy livestock all contribute to the problem. The consequences are already visible in hospitals, where certain infections no longer respond to even the strongest drugs. Meanwhile, the pipeline of new antibiotics has nearly dried up, because pharmaceutical companies earn little from medicines that are taken for only a few days. Health experts insist that the solution lies in stewardship: using these drugs only when necessary, completing every prescribed course, and rewarding the development of new ones.

Question: Why do resistant strains of bacteria emerge faster when an antibiotic is used more frequently?

options.text: Antibiotics themselves create new bacteria
Bacteria stop multiplying when exposed to the drug
Frequent use makes the human body resistant
Each use lets a few chance survivors pass their resistance on to their offspring

explanation: पैसेज के अनुसार हर बार दवा के प्रयोग पर कुछ जीवाणु संयोगवश (mutation) बच जाते हैं और अपनी प्रतिरोधक क्षमता अपनी संतानों को दे देते हैं; इसलिए जितना अधिक प्रयोग, उतनी तेज़ी से resistant strains बनते हैं।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
A few decades ago, public opinion was shaped by a handful of newspapers and broadcasters, whose editors acted as gatekeepers deciding which events deserved the nation's attention. Social media has swept this arrangement away. Anyone with a phone can now publish a view to thousands of strangers, and ideas that once struggled to find a hearing can spread within hours. This has undoubtedly broadened the public conversation, giving a voice to groups long ignored by the mainstream press. Yet the same openness carries a hidden cost. Because platforms earn money by holding our attention, their algorithms tend to promote content that provokes strong emotion, and outrage travels faster than nuance. Users are also shown more of what they already agree with, so that disagreement begins to look like ignorance or malice. The result is not a conversation but a series of parallel monologues. Media literacy, the habit of questioning the source and intent of what one reads, is therefore no longer a specialised skill but a civic necessity, as essential to a citizen as the ability to read itself.

Question: What role did editors play in shaping public opinion in the past, according to the passage?

options.text: They acted as gatekeepers deciding which events deserved the nation's attention
They allowed anyone to publish an opinion
They promoted content that provoked outrage
They taught readers media literacy

explanation: पैसेज के अनुसार पहले संपादक 'gatekeeper' की भूमिका निभाते थे और तय करते थे कि किन घटनाओं पर देश का ध्यान जाना चाहिए।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
A few decades ago, public opinion was shaped by a handful of newspapers and broadcasters, whose editors acted as gatekeepers deciding which events deserved the nation's attention. Social media has swept this arrangement away. Anyone with a phone can now publish a view to thousands of strangers, and ideas that once struggled to find a hearing can spread within hours. This has undoubtedly broadened the public conversation, giving a voice to groups long ignored by the mainstream press. Yet the same openness carries a hidden cost. Because platforms earn money by holding our attention, their algorithms tend to promote content that provokes strong emotion, and outrage travels faster than nuance. Users are also shown more of what they already agree with, so that disagreement begins to look like ignorance or malice. The result is not a conversation but a series of parallel monologues. Media literacy, the habit of questioning the source and intent of what one reads, is therefore no longer a specialised skill but a civic necessity, as essential to a citizen as the ability to read itself.

Question: What does the author mean by 'parallel monologues'?

options.text: Two groups debate each other fairly
Platforms show the same content to everyone
Users post identical messages at the same time
People speak without genuinely listening to opposing views

explanation: पैसेज के अनुसार उपयोगकर्ताओं को वही दिखाया जाता है जिससे वे पहले से सहमत हैं, इसलिए संवाद के बजाय सब अपनी-अपनी बात कहते हैं और विरोधी मत सुनते नहीं; यही 'parallel monologues' है।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
Many parents believe that sending a child to an English-medium school from the earliest age is the surest route to success, and that the mother tongue is a handicap to be outgrown. Research on learning, however, suggests that the opposite may be closer to the truth. Children grasp new concepts most readily in the language they speak at home, because they do not have to struggle with words while trying to understand ideas. A child who has built a firm foundation in her first language finds it easier, not harder, to acquire a second one, since the basic principles of grammar and expression carry over from one language to another. By contrast, a child who is forced to learn everything in an unfamiliar language often memorises answers without understanding them, and such learning is shallow and quickly forgotten. This does not mean that English should be neglected; proficiency in it opens doors to higher education and employment. It means only that the sequence matters. A language should be added to a child's mind, not substituted for the one already there.

Question: According to the passage, why do children grasp new concepts most readily in their home language?

options.text: The grammar of the home language is simpler than that of other languages
Teachers speak only the home language
They do not have to struggle with words while trying to understand ideas
They are not required to learn anything else

explanation: पैसेज के अनुसार घर की भाषा में बच्चों को शब्दों से जूझना नहीं पड़ता, इसलिए वे विचारों को समझने पर पूरा ध्यान दे पाते हैं।
